title: Using PEP more than once
answer: PEP can be given again if you have another possible HIV exposure, and a health worker will not refuse you because you used it before. But PEP is an emergency medicine, not a regular prevention method. If you keep needing PEP, it means you are at ongoing risk, and PrEP together with condoms may protect you better. Talk to a health worker about your options without fear of being judged.

title: Getting PEP without a parent
answer: Young people in Rwanda aged 12 and older can consent to HIV testing on their own, and PEP is started after an HIV test, so a parent should not be a barrier to getting urgent care. Go straight to a health facility within 72 hours and explain what happened. Health workers will keep your information private. If you can, bring a trusted adult for support, but do not delay.

title: Care after rape besides PEP
answer: After rape, PEP is only one part of care. At a health facility or Isange One Stop Centre (call 3029), you can also get emergency contraception to prevent pregnancy, tests and treatment for other STIs, care for injuries, counselling, and help with police and legal support if you choose. Follow-up visits are important. You deserve care and support, and what happened was not your fault.

title: Does PEP always work
answer: PEP greatly lowers the chance of getting HIV when it is started early and taken every day for all 28 days, but it is not 100 percent effective. It works best when started within hours, not days. That is why follow-up HIV tests are needed after finishing. Keep using condoms during and after PEP until your follow-up tests are done.

answer: Children who have been sexually abused can and should get PEP if it is within 72 hours, along with other care. Take the child to the nearest health facility or Isange One Stop Centre as soon as possible, or call 3029 or the child helpline 116. Health workers know how to care for children gently. The child needs comfort, safety and to hear that it is not their fault.

title: What ART is
answer: ART stands for antiretroviral therapy. It is the medicine people living with HIV take every day to control the virus. ART stops HIV from making copies of itself, which lets the immune system recover and protects the person from getting sick. It does not cure HIV, but when taken well it allows people to live long, healthy lives and stops HIV from passing to sexual partners.

title: Starting ART on the day of diagnosis
answer: In Rwanda, everyone diagnosed with HIV is offered treatment, no matter their CD4 count, and many people can start ART on the same day or within a few days of diagnosis, once they are ready. Starting early protects your immune system and your partners. The health worker will counsel you and check for illnesses like TB first. If you need time, talk openly about it.

title: Why ART is for life
answer: ART controls HIV but does not remove it from the body. The virus hides in some cells, and if you stop treatment it comes back and starts damaging the immune system again. That is why ART is taken every day for life. Many people find it becomes a normal daily habit, like brushing teeth. Your health worker will support you along the way.

title: Why taking ART every day matters
answer: Taking ART every day, as your health worker advised, is called adherence. It keeps enough medicine in your blood to stop HIV from multiplying. When doses are often missed, the virus can grow again and may become resistant, meaning the medicine stops working. Good adherence keeps you healthy, makes your viral load undetectable, and protects your partners.

title: Missing a dose of ART

title: Side effects of ART
answer: Most people take ART with few or no problems. Some have mild side effects at first, such as nausea, headache, tiredness, dizziness or strange dreams, which often improve within weeks. Do not stop your medicine because of side effects. Tell your health worker, who can help manage them or change the medicine if needed. Go to a health facility quickly if you have a serious rash, yellow eyes or feel very ill.

title: Stopping ART when you feel well
answer: Feeling well is a sign that ART is working, not that HIV is gone. If you stop your medicine, the virus will multiply again, your immune system will weaken, you can pass HIV to others, and the virus may become resistant. Never stop ART without talking to your health worker. If something makes it hard to continue, they can help.

title: HIV drug resistance
answer: Drug resistance happens when HIV changes so that a medicine no longer works against it. It usually develops when ART is taken irregularly or stopped and started. Resistant HIV is harder to treat and may need different medicines. You can prevent resistance by taking your ART every day as advised and going for your viral load tests.

title: What a viral load test is
answer: A viral load test measures how much HIV is in your blood. It shows whether your ART is working. The goal is a very low or undetectable viral load. In Rwanda, people on ART have viral load tests at regular times set by the guidelines. Your health worker will explain your results and what to do if the viral load is high.

title: Undetectable equals untransmittable
answer: When a person living with HIV takes ART every day and their viral load stays undetectable, they do not pass HIV to their sexual partners. This is called U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable. Their viral load must be confirmed by a test and they must keep taking treatment. U=U is about sexual transmission; it does not protect against other STIs or pregnancy.

answer: Most people who take ART every day reach an undetectable viral load within a few months, often by about six months. Your health worker will test your viral load to confirm. answer: A high viral load result while on ART means the virus is not fully controlled. The most common reason is missed doses, but other causes include vomiting, other medicines, or resistance. title: Herbal medicine and ART
answer: Some herbal or traditional medicines can interfere with ART, making it work less well or causing side effects. Herbs cannot replace ART. Before taking any herbs, supplements or other medicines, tell your health worker. Never stop your ART to try herbal treatment.

title: Alcohol and drugs while on ART
answer: Alcohol and drugs can make you forget your ART doses, harm your liver, and lead to unsafe sex. Heavy drinking is especially harmful. If you drink, make sure you still take your medicine on time. If you find it hard to control alcohol or drug use, talk honestly with your health worker; they can help without judging you.

title: Life expectancy with HIV on treatment
answer: Today, a young person who starts ART early and takes it every day can expect to live a long life, close to that of people without HIV. They can finish school, work, marry and have children. title: Condoms when you are undetectable
answer: An undetectable viral load means you do not pass HIV through sex. answer: Never share your ARVs with anyone or take someone else's. Sharing means you will run short and miss doses, which can cause resistance.
